scenes.title: Explain the architecture at the right level
scenes.text: A Component diagram describes software structure and the services or infrastructure that connect it. It is useful when an audience needs to understand responsibilities and dependencies without reading a sequence of individual messages. Our portal has a web app, API, request database, notification queue and worker. We will create another component, inspect infrastructure kinds and interfaces, group the architecture, and apply a shared style. State what a connection means rather than treating every arrow as an interchangeable line.
scenes.source:
@startuml
title Customer portal architecture
component "Web app" as Web
component API
component "Notification worker" as Worker
queue "Notification queue" as Queue
database "Request database" as Database
Web --> API : HTTPS
API --> Database : read / write
API --> Queue : request created
Queue --> Worker : process event
@enduml

actions.title: Explain the system’s major building blocks

scenes.title: Create a component or infrastructure object
scenes.text: Choose Component or infrastructure from Insert and add an Audit service. Review the kind options: the editor also supports interfaces, databases, queues, clouds, nodes, artifacts, files, folders and rectangles. Choose the kind for what the object represents in this view. A database or deployment node is not the same concept as a software component. Inspect the resulting declaration and give the object a stable alias when other statements will refer to it.

scenes.title: Inspect identity and placement
scenes.text: Select API and open its inspector. Kind, name and alias identify the object, while stereotype and color describe presentation or classification. Container placement groups it within a package or node. These fields answer different questions, so avoid changing them all merely to make the drawing fit. Inspect the source after an identity change and verify the connections. The same common editor pattern applies here as in Class diagrams, but the modeled meaning is architectural rather than a member-level type design.

actions.value: Identity, classification and deployment placement are different decisions.

scenes.title: Make the service boundary explicit
scenes.text: The reference example adds a Request service interface beside API. An interface helps explain what another component relies on, while the API implementation remains a separate object. Read the declaration and connection together, and decide how much detail is useful for this audience. Do not imply an implemented protocol simply because two objects are next to each other. Use a label or note to state the relevant interaction or contract, and keep that explanation consistent with the Sequence model.

scenes.title: Inspect dependency endpoints and meaning
scenes.text: Open Relationship to inspect the supported kinds and endpoint controls. In our example, Web uses API over HTTPS, API reads and writes the database, and notifications move through the queue to the worker. Those labels explain different interactions. Reconnect an incorrectly chosen endpoint rather than leaving a misleading architectural dependency. Check the source after reordering or moving an object into a container so that the intended structure remains intact.

scenes.title: Packages, nodes and notes
scenes.text: A package or node groups related objects, but the kind of grouping matters. The extended example puts the web app in a browser environment and records an assumption at the API boundary. Compare these declarations with the preview, then inspect package creation and Diagram settings. A deployment node, ownership grouping and logical package can answer different questions. Keep a boundary explicit enough that a reader does not have to guess whether it means physical location, ownership or software structure.

scenes.title: Style a component category
scenes.text: Select Web and API together and inspect the bulk styling controls. Apply one shared style to distinguish a category of software objects. Styling should support names and boundaries, not become the only way to understand them. Review the source after the bulk change and check copied or duplicated objects for unintended identifiers or connections. The source history provides a way to reconsider the operation when the selected set was too broad.

scenes.title: Explain the notification path
scenes.text: Pause and add an Audit service. Identify the request database, notification queue and worker as distinct responsibilities, then explain the path from request creation to notification processing. Add one interface and one boundary that have a clear meaning in your model. Inspect a connection, add an explanatory note and style a verified pair of components. A successful result can be explained without pretending that this structural diagram is a complete timeline of runtime behavior.

scenes.title: Choose the view for the question
scenes.text: Components, infrastructure, interfaces and boundaries help explain the system's major structure. Use messages or workflow models for the detailed behavior that this diagram does not show. Keep aliases, endpoint meaning and grouping deliberate, and use notes to state relevant assumptions. The next lesson models a request intake workflow with decisions, loops and parallel work, moving from structural responsibilities back to the order and conditions of behavior.
